seo.title: Karmic tail 12 10 7 compatibility: who holds the reins
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 10 7 compatibility: the couple enters its task by yielding, lives through turns of fortune and learns to drive together, read through Persuasion.

title: The couple's karmic tail 12-10-7: The Hanged Man, The Wheel of Fortune and The Chariot in compatibility
short: A man hanging upside down who does not move. A wheel that turns by itself. A chariot that someone drives. The three cards of the couple's karmic tail 12-10-7 are three ways of standing still and travelling, and in this order they make a plot: the couple enters its task by yielding and waiting, goes through it by way of turns that come from outside, and the main task is to take the reins and drive on together, leaving the road neither to chance nor to one of the two.

sections.h2: A novel written to these three cards
paragraphs: In 1806 Anne Elliot, nineteen, becomes engaged to a young naval officer, Frederick Wentworth. He has no fortune and no connections, only the certainty that everything will come. Lady Russell, who has taken the place of Anne's mother, persuades her to break the engagement, and Anne gives way. Wentworth goes to sea. Eight years later he comes back a captain and a rich man, while Anne's father, having run through his money, lets the family estate — to Wentworth's sister and her husband, an admiral. The two sit in the same drawing room again, and neither can speak first.

This is the last novel Jane Austen finished, Persuasion; Russian readers know it as Dovody rassudka ("The Arguments of Reason"), in Elena Surits's translation. Austen completed it in the summer of 1816, and the book came out after her death, in December 1817. The title was given by her brother Henry; she herself, by family tradition, called the novel The Elliots. The word left on the cover means both "being talked round" and "conviction", and it describes the first card of the tail. Austen is quoted here in her own English.

In the fourth chapter there is a sentence in which the three cards stand side by side. Anne, at twenty-seven, thinks how eloquent she could now be on the side of "early warm attachment, and a cheerful confidence in futurity, against that over-anxious caution which seems to insult exertion and distrust Providence". The caution that does not move is The Hanged Man. The Providence it distrusts is The Wheel: Waite writes that behind its turns stands Providence, not chance. The exertion it insults is The Chariot.

The next sentence is a portrait of The Hanged Man: **"She had been forced into prudence in her youth, she learned romance as she grew older: the natural sequel of an unnatural beginning."** A life turned upside down: first the caution that suits old age, then the daring that suits youth.

The whole novel runs in the order of the tail. First the persuasion and eight years of standing still. Then the wheel of fortune, which lifts one and lowers the other. At the end, the question of who will take the reins. Austen answers it twice: with a gig in which another couple is driving, and with a letter the hero writes himself.

In the novel the woman gives way and the man holds out: that was the choice of the age and of the author. In a couple with the tail 12-10-7 the roles are not tied to sex and easily change places, and often both live in one person.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: a sacrifice nobody asked for
paragraphs: Point M in the couple's matrix is the "Entry to the task": what the two want together and the language in which they come to terms. On the couple's chart the same point also stands in the sphere "Relationship and common language". The Hanged Man here is a shared wish to protect each other at the cost of one's own step: to wait, to give way, not to drag the other into risk. This wish brings the couple into the task, and it also becomes the resistance.

Anne does not break off the engagement out of calculation. "The belief of being prudent, and self-denying, principally for his advantage, was her chief consolation." The key word is "his". A decision about two was taken by one, out of love, and handed to the other as a finished fact. Wentworth answers with what Anne did not expect: he does not forgive. She had, he thinks, "shewn a feebleness of character in doing so, which his own decided, confident temper could not endure. She had given him up to oblige others."

The striking thing is that Wentworth speaks the same language. On principle he takes no women aboard his ship, "from feeling how impossible it is, with all one's efforts, and all one's sacrifices, to make the accommodations on board such as women ought to have". His sister cuts him short: "All idle refinement!" The two say the same thing in different words: protect the other by keeping them off the road. This is the common language of a couple with The Hanged Man at the entry.

And then both of them hang. Anne refuses another suitor, Charles Musgrove, though Lady Russell would have been glad of the match. Wentworth returns to England in 1808 with a few thousand pounds and does not write to her. Later he admits: "I was proud, too proud to ask again." His letter will give the exact term — "eight years and a half". Nobody leaves, and nobody comes forward. A pause for two that nobody announced.

Waite argues with the prudent reading of The Hanged Man too. This card, he writes, "is supposed to represent Prudence", and he rejects that reading along with martyrdom and duty. His divinatory list for the card gives "Wisdom, circumspection, discernment, trials, sacrifice". Anne's prudence did indeed turn out to be not wisdom but a life in suspension: she plays the pianoforte so that others can dance, and "desired nothing in return but to be unobserved".

In Lisovskaya's book on compatibility The Hanged Man in the plus means tact, attention, a readiness to give way. The partners sense each other at a distance, take a long time to enter a relationship, and need a push from outside to marry. In a couple today it looks like this. One keeps quiet about a job offer in another city, "so as not to make her choose". The other puts off her studies "because now is not the time". Both wait until it is convenient and live for years inside the pause. The minus of the same entry: decisions taken "because that is how it has to be", a glance over the shoulder at what the family will say, and the weariness of the one who holds the relationship together with all their strength and gets reproaches in return.

The Hanged Man also has a way of speaking. In the novel the most important words are almost always said to a third person. Anne sits by a hedgerow and hears Wentworth explaining to Louisa Musgrove what firmness is. Later it is he who listens while Anne talks about constancy with his friend. A couple with this tail also slips easily into a language of hints, errands and "I thought you'd understand without being told".

sections.h2: Middle of the task: a wheel that moves the two around
paragraphs: Point N is the "Middle of the task". In Lisovskaya it has no meaning of its own, only adding to the main task; in our reading it shows how the couple lives the road from the entry to the goal. The Wheel of Fortune in the middle means the road runs through turns that come from outside and each time change where the two stand.

In English, fortune means both luck and wealth, and Austen plays on the word throughout the novel. In 1806 "Captain Wentworth had no fortune." But "he had always been lucky; he knew he should be so still." The war with Napoleon brings prize money: by the end of the novel he has twenty-five thousand pounds. Meanwhile Anne's father, the baronet Sir Walter, lives beyond his means and has to let the estate — to Admiral Croft, a sailor made rich by the same war. Sir Walter complains that the navy is "raising men to honours which their fathers and grandfathers never dreamt of". It is a complaint against the Wheel itself.

Waite's list for The Wheel reads like Wentworth's service record: "Destiny, fortune, success, elevation, luck, felicity." Even The Wheel reversed is not failure for Waite but "Increase, abundance, superfluity": superfluity is what ruined Sir Walter.

Wen adds one more face to The Wheel: force majeure, "an 'act of god,' chance occurrence, unavoidable accident, or matter beyond the Seeker's control", which changes the outcome. In the novel it happens at Lyme. On the stone breakwater Louisa Musgrove runs back up the steps so that Wentworth can catch her jump once more. He advises against it, she answers "I am determined I will", jumps half a second before he can catch her — "too precipitate by half a second" — and falls senseless on the stones. Louisa will recover, but it is this fall that rearranges events. While she slowly comes round, another captain, Benwick, is at hand, and Louisa marries him. Austen explains the match in one sentence: "It had been in situation." Wentworth is free — not because he decided it himself.

The same turn has a second side: it shows who is who. Over Louisa, Wentworth cries, "Is there no one to help me?" — and it is Anne, the one who always gave way, who starts giving orders. Charles Musgrove keeps repeating, "Anne, Anne, what is to be done next?", and "both seemed to look to her for directions". At the turn of the wheel the yielding partner takes the reins. Among Lisovskaya's examples for this energy are couples in which one pulled the other out of a crisis.

Anne herself, at the end of the novel, states the law of The Wheel. Lady Russell's advice, she says, was "one of those cases in which advice is good or bad only as the event decides". A decision is taken in one position of the wheel and judged in another. Hence the minus of the middle. The couple blames fate and each other after the fact: "if only you had…". The swing of "silence, then a row" begins; it is hard together, yet something holds them. The plus is a feeling of a fated meeting and the ability to accept the partner in any position. The wheel turns for everyone; it is just that for this couple the turns stand right on the road to the task: one partner's promotion and the other's redundancy, a move, the birth of a child, the parents' decision to sell the country house. Every turn asks again who is on top now and who is driving.

Point D is the "Main task": the couple's chief trials, read above all through the minus. The Chariot is direction and will, movement towards where you have decided to go. A couple with this tail is learning not decisiveness in general but decisiveness for two.

Wentworth at the start of the novel is The Chariot in the minus. He resents "a feebleness of character" and looks for its opposite. In that scene by the hedgerow he tells Louisa: "It is the worst evil of too yielding and indecisive a character, that no influence over it can be depended on… Let those who would be happy be firm." He picks a nut from a bough, one that "has outlived all the storms of autumn", and holds it up as an example. Two chapters later firm Louisa jumps from the steps because she has decided to.

Wentworth draws the lesson himself, and Austen records it in a sentence that could serve as the definition of this tail's main task: at Lyme **"he had learnt to distinguish between the steadiness of principle and the obstinacy of self-will, between the darings of heedlessness and the resolution of a collected mind"**.

Waite calls the charioteer "above all things triumph in the mind", yet his divinatory list for The Chariot does not begin with victory. The first words are "Succour, providence", and only then "war, triumph, presumption, vengeance, trouble". Wentworth has both halves. When Anne's little nephew hangs on her neck, Wentworth silently lifts the boy off and walks away without waiting for thanks. When Anne tires on a walk, he puts her into his sister's gig, and she feels "that his will and his hands had done it". And the same man nurses a grievance for eight years and writes of himself honestly in his letter: "weak and resentful I have been".

Lisovskaya finds the trials of The Chariot in a couple where the two share the reins. In 1806 Anne and Wentworth ran into all of them at once: his career or their marriage, her family or his road — and the question of who would sacrifice whom was settled by one of them. Today the same trials look ordinary. One partner is offered work abroad, and the question "shall we go?" is talked over for so long that the deadline for an answer decides for both. One expects the other to drop their studies or their business because his or her own goal is "more important for the family". The two plan a holiday, a renovation or a child, and the quarrel over who is in charge flares up out of nothing. Or the reverse: nobody drives, and the couple rolls wherever the road happens to tilt. Lisovskaya's advice for this energy is to name the status of the relationship and the roles clearly, leaving nothing unsaid, and not to hurry the partner.

sections.h2: The Crofts' gig: a task solved before the novel begins
paragraphs: In the novel there is a couple whose main task in this tail is already solved — Admiral Croft and his wife Sophy, Wentworth's sister. Austen shows them in the very gig into which Wentworth has put the tired Anne.

On the way the Admiral recalls his own courtship: "How many days was it, my dear, between the first time of my seeing you and our sitting down together in our lodgings at North Yarmouth?" Mrs Croft replies that they had better not talk about it: if Miss Elliot heard how soon they came to an understanding, "she would never be persuaded that we could be happy together". The same word again, this time with a smile.

And then the gig nearly runs into a post. "My dear Admiral, that post! we shall certainly take that post." Austen goes on: "But by coolly giving the reins a better direction herself they happily passed the danger; and by once afterwards judiciously putting out her hand they neither fell into a rut, nor ran foul of a dung-cart; **and Anne, with some amusement at their style of driving, which she imagined no bad representation of the general guidance of their affairs, found herself safely deposited by them at the Cottage.**" This is not a tarot reader talking but Austen herself: the gig is a portrait of a marriage.

The Chariot of a couple in the plus looks exactly like this. The reins are with one, but the other sits alongside, watches the road and calmly corrects. Nobody is a passenger, nobody is in command for all occasions. Mrs Croft has sailed with her husband for fifteen years, has "crossed the Atlantic four times", and tells her brother: "I hate to hear you talking so like a fine gentleman, and as if women were all fine ladies, instead of rational creatures. We none of us expect to be in smooth water all our days." There will be no smooth water, because The Wheel sits in the middle of the tail. The task is not to stop it but to ride it together.

In Bath Anne sees the Crofts in every street. They walk "in happy independence", and Mrs Croft stands in a knot of naval officers "looking as intelligent and keen as any of the officers around her". This matches how Lisovskaya describes The Chariot of a couple in the plus: more a team and friends than a couple, active, ready to set off, deciding together and fast.

sections.h2: A letter instead of an errand: how Austen rewrote the ending
paragraphs: In the summer of 1816 Austen finished the novel with a different scene. Admiral Croft drags Anne into his lodgings, leaves her alone with Wentworth, and behind the door demands that his brother-in-law find out from her whether it is true she is to marry her cousin. "I hate to be at an uncertainty. I must know at once," says the Admiral. "If you will not speak, I will stop and speak myself." Wentworth does speak, but, in his own words, "speaking only for another, and speaking by necessity". The explanation happens, the couple is united — by a push from outside, the very push without which, in Lisovskaya, The Hanged Man finds it hard to reach marriage.

Austen was not satisfied with the scene. Her nephew James Edward Austen-Leigh writes in his Memoir of Jane Austen that his aunt "thought it tame and flat", went to bed one night in low spirits, and in the morning cancelled the chapter and wrote two new ones in its place. The rejected chapter survived in manuscript and was later printed, so it can be set beside the final one.

In the new ending there is no push. At the inn Anne argues with Captain Harville about who loves more constantly, men or women, and says: "All the privilege I claim for my own sex (it is not a very enviable one; you need not covet it), is that of loving longest, when existence or when hope is gone." At the next table Wentworth is writing what everyone takes for a letter to Benwick. He leaves without a look at Anne, comes back "for his gloves", draws another letter from under the papers and places it before her. "I can listen no longer in silence. I must speak to you by such means as are within my reach. You pierce my soul. I am half agony, half hope… Unjust I may have been, weak and resentful I have been, but never inconstant."

The Hanged Man is still there: the letter is written, not spoken, and the pretext is a pair of forgotten gloves. But the errand is gone; he has taken the reins himself. Anne, holding the letter, feels that "anything might be defied rather than suspense". Austen rewrote the ending exactly the way this tail rewrites a couple: from a push from outside to a step of one's own.

Then the two walk along a quiet gravel path, "as they slowly paced the gradual ascent", and Austen sums up: they are now "more fixed in a knowledge of each other's character" and **"more equal to act, more justified in acting"**. Each owns their part. Anne does not disown the past: giving way to Lady Russell, she says, was right, or her conscience would have tormented her. Wentworth admits that his worst enemy was himself. He asks whether she would have answered if he had written to her in the year eight. "Would I!" — and nothing more is needed. His last words in that chapter are The Chariot finally coming to terms with The Wheel: "I have been used to the gratification of believing myself to earn every blessing that I enjoyed… I must endeavour to subdue my mind to my fortune. I must learn to brook being happier than I deserve."

sections.h2: Waite and Wen: the three cards pass the baton
paragraphs: Books on tarot know nothing of matrix tails, yet in them these three cards are linked in the same order.

Wen ends The Hanged Man reversed like this: "It is not for the Seeker to administer judgment, vengeance, or penance. **Let the Wheel of Fortune turn on its own accord.**" The card of the entry names the card of the middle itself. The Wheel reversed, for Wen, describes "a person who cannot rely on predetermined or external forces to sweep in and help support him or her", a message "to exert greater willpower". And The Chariot, in her words, "indicates great control over one's willpower". The Hanged Man lets The Wheel go, The Wheel demands will, and will is the essence of The Chariot.

Waite links the middle and the task with a single word. Of The Wheel he writes that behind it "there lies the denial of chance" and that its letters are there "to shew that Providence is implied through all". His divinatory list for The Chariot opens with "Succour, providence". The charioteer does not argue with The Wheel; he carries it on with his own hands. Austen said the same: the caution that would "distrust Providence" also "insults exertion".

On Waite's cards there is also a shared beast. At the top of his Wheel sits a sphinx with a sword, and Waite explains: "The Sphinx is the equilibrium therein", "stability amidst movement". Waite's Chariot is drawn by two sphinxes, because the charioteer "has thus replied to the sphinx". The riddle that sits on top of The Wheel is harnessed to The Chariot and pulls it. The cards of our deck are drawn differently; this detail belongs to Waite's deck.

Of The Hanged Man Waite reminds us that "the tree of sacrifice is living wood", and that the figure "suggests life in suspension, but life and not death". Anne's eight years are exactly that kind of life. She did not die to love; she hung.

sections.h2: The numbers of tail 12-10-7: what is written in the couple's cards
paragraphs: The tail 12-10-7 occurs in roughly one couple in 122 (0.822%) and ranks 45th of the 97 couple tails — almost the middle of the list. No other couple tail is made of these three numbers: not 7-10-12, not 10-12-7, no other order. This plot reads in one direction only.

Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22: if the sum is larger, its digits are added. The couple's middle is added up from the partners' middles, not from the two outer numbers. That is why 12-10-7 occurs only in a couple. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the entry plus the task: 12 + 7 = 19, The Sun, and that personal tail, 12-19-7, exists. So one person goes from The Hanged Man to The Chariot through The Sun, through being seen and through a clear day of their own. Two people take the same road through The Wheel.

The couple's Hanged Man never comes from either partner's personal entry. It is made of other cards: The Moon and The World (18 + 21 = 39 → 12) in 41.1% of such couples, The Empress and The Hermit (3 + 9) in 37.5%, two Lovers (6 + 6) in 21.3%. In one couple in five The Hanged Man is put together by two people who each enter their own tail through The Lovers, that is, through choice. Two choices made towards each other produce suspension: so it was with Anne and Wentworth in 1806.

The Wheel in the couple's middle is also always the sum of two personal middles, and neither partner has a Wheel of their own there. In 34% of such couples one of the two terms is The Chariot: one partner has their own will, their own drive, in the middle of their personal tail, and together with the other's Empress it turns into The Wheel. One person's will becomes, for the two of them, a turn of fate. Wentworth's career was The Chariot for him and a wheel of fortune for Anne: first it took her fiancé away, then it brought him back rich.

The tail belongs to the couple as a whole. The Hanged Man stands in the personal tail of at least one partner in only 14.8% of such couples, The Wheel in 26.3%, The Chariot in 34%. In 39.7% of couples none of the three cards appears in either partner's personal tail: neither brought this plot along; it is born between them.

sections.h2: Atmosphere and values: Temperance, The Hierophant, The Lovers, The Devil
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's chart is the shared atmosphere, what lies between the two and is not on show. In 88.7% of 12-10-7 couples the centre holds Temperance. In the plus these are quarrels settled by talking and compromise, and the ability to wait for the right moment — the good version of The Hanged Man. In the minus Lisovskaya describes Temperance in one phrase that fits the first half of the novel: one always gives way, and the other never even thinks about it. Her advice for this energy — not to jump to conclusions about the partner — Wentworth broke after their very first meeting, deciding that Anne was "so altered that he should not have known her again".

In 11.3% of couples the centre holds The Hierophant. In its minus Lisovskaya names the family's interference, up to the choice of a partner — the part played by Lady Russell, who had towards Anne "almost a mother's love, and mother's rights". Only with The Hierophant does the couple's entry follow the personal formula, task plus centre: 7 + 5 = 12.

"The couple's values" are what the union exists for. In 58.4% of 12-10-7 couples they are The Lovers, in 41.6% The Devil. Our reading: The Lovers are a choice that has to be made a second time, as adults and in another position of the wheel, like Anne's "Would I!". The Devil is an attachment that does not let go for eight years, and the question of whether the couple is held by free choice or by a chain of other people's opinions and their own pride. Lisovskaya sums this energy up in the words "no one belongs to anyone".

sections.h2: How to work out the couple's tail: example 05.12.1975 and 07.01.1976
paragraphs: The partner born on 05.12.1975 has the personal tail 18-3-12, the partner born on 07.01.1976 has 21-7-13. The points are added pair by pair:

This example shows how the tail is assembled from other cards. For the first partner The Hanged Man is the personal main task, but in the couple's tail it becomes one of the terms and, together with the second partner's Death, gives The Chariot (12 + 13). For the second partner The Chariot stands in the middle of the personal tail, and in the couple, together with the first partner's Empress, it turns into The Wheel (3 + 7).

This couple's centre is Temperance (6 + 8 = 14), and "The couple's values" hold The Devil. The Hanged Man repeats on the "Image of the couple": from outside, too, the two are seen as people who give way and look after each other, which happens in 6.4% of couples with this tail. The Chariot repeats on the point "What fills", which happens in 6.6% of such couples. This couple's main task is also its fuel: Lisovskaya writes that The Chariot fills a union with the road, with a move to a place chosen together and with the partner's successes, when the two walk side by side but each on their own path.

The tail does not predict how many years the pause will last or whether there will be a "Lyme". It shows where the couple usually keeps the wheel and who lets go of it. Here is what the novel and the cards suggest.

ul: **Offer the sacrifice, do not make it.** If one partner has decided to step back "for the other's good", ask the other first. Anne decided for two, Wentworth decided for every woman on his ship, and both made the same mistake.

**Speak for yourselves, not through a go-between.** Austen struck out the ending in which the Admiral speaks for the hero. Hints, errands and "you should have known" are the language of The Hanged Man; the task of The Chariot is a plain sentence.

**Do not judge a past decision by the wheel's present position.** Advice is good or bad "only as the event decides". The reproach "if only you had…" is an argument with The Wheel, not with the partner.
**In a crisis, watch who keeps a cool head.** A turn often changes the roles: the one who always gave way suddenly takes charge. That change is worth noticing and not taking away.
**Test the firmness.** "Steadiness of principle or obstinacy of self-will?" is a question worth asking oneself before every "I am determined I will".
**Name the route out loud.** Where are we going, who is driving now, when do we change over. A move, a job, a child, a big purchase are decisions for two, not concessions by one.
**Take each other along rather than shield each other from the road.** "We none of us expect to be in smooth water all our days."

paragraphs: The Chariot in the minus can also be heavy: control over every step, bans, threats. That is no longer a lesson of the tail to be endured but a reason to seek help — a psychologist, a crisis line, and in danger the local emergency number.

The strong version of the tail 12-10-7 is the Crofts in their gig. The two know how to wait and how to give way, but no longer mistake this for standing still. The Wheel turns, and the reins are shared.

ul: **M · Entry to the task — The Hanged Man (12).** The couple's common language is to give way, to wait it out, to give up one's own move for the other's sake. With this wish the couple enters the task, and the same wish holds it back.

**N · Middle of the task — The Wheel of Fortune (10).** The road runs through changes the two do not control: money, work, other people's decisions, chance. The Wheel moves the partners around, and each time they meet in a new position.

**D · Main task — The Chariot (7).** To decide and to go together: to name the direction, to agree on who is driving now, and to tell firmness from stubbornness. In the minus, the two either stand still or each pulls the reins their own way.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 12-10-7 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the task of a couple that begins with yielding and waiting (The Hanged Man at the entry), goes through turns of circumstance (The Wheel of Fortune in the middle) and learns to choose the direction together and drive together (The Chariot as the main task). The main trial is to tell firmness from stubbornness and not to decide for the other.

faq.q: Why does the tail 12-10-7 occur only in a couple?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the entry plus the main task: with 12 and 7 it would be 19, The Sun. In a couple the middle is added up from the two partners' middles, which is why it comes out as 10 here. The tail 12-10-7 does not occur in a personal matrix.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. Among the 97 couple tails, the cards 12, 10 and 7 make only the order 12-10-7. The engine gives no other permutation, such as 7-10-12, for any pair of dates.

faq.q: Does this tail mean the couple is bound to wait a long time or to part?
faq.a: No. The tail describes a task, not events or dates. It shows the language in which the couple is used to giving way, how it lives through change and what it has to learn in shared decisions. How long the pause lasts and how the turn ends is up to the two of them.

It occurs in roughly one couple in 122, which is 0.822% of all couples and 45th place of the 97 couple tails. Most often it forms between partners with the personal tails 18-6-15 and 21-4-10, 3-7-22 and 9-3-21, 3-22-19 and 9-15-6.

The plot of the novel runs in the same order. In 1806 Anne, nineteen, becomes engaged to a sailor, Frederick Wentworth, who has neither fortune nor connections. report.h3: A wheel that moves the two around

report: The middle of the tail is The Wheel of Fortune: the road runs through turns that come from outside. In English, fortune means both luck and wealth. The war makes Wentworth rich, Anne's father is ruined, and a sailor moves into his estate. Every turn puts the two in a new position.

A turn also shows who is who. When Louisa Musgrove falls on the stone breakwater, Wentworth cries, "Is there no one to help me?" — and it is Anne, the one who always gave way, who starts giving orders. **At the turn of the wheel the yielding partner takes the reins.** Anne herself later states the law of this card: Lady Russell's advice was "one of those cases in which advice is good or bad only as the event decides". A decision is taken in one position of the wheel and judged in another. Hence the minus of the middle: "if only…", the swing between silence and rows, resentment against fate and against each other.

Benebell Wen links these cards almost on purpose. She ends The Hanged Man reversed with the words "Let the Wheel of Fortune turn on its own accord", and her Wheel reversed calls on the Seeker "to exert greater willpower". Will is the essence of The Chariot.

report.h3: Steadiness of principle or obstinacy of self-will

report: The main task is The Chariot: to decide and to go together. At first Wentworth mistakes it for stubbornness. He has not forgiven Anne "a feebleness of character" and lectures Louisa: "Let those who would be happy be firm." Two chapters later firm Louisa jumps from the steps because she has decided to. After that, Austen writes, **"he had learnt to distinguish between the steadiness of principle and the obstinacy of self-will, between the darings of heedlessness and the resolution of a collected mind"**. This sentence holds the whole main task of the tail 12-10-7. In the minus the two either stand still or each pulls the reins their own way: whose work matters more, whether to move together, who decides about the renovation and the child.

Austen shows the task solved in another couple, Admiral Croft and his wife. They are driving a gig; she spots a post, coolly gives the reins a better direction herself and takes them past the danger. Anne thinks their style of driving is "no bad representation of the general guidance of their affairs". Mrs Croft has crossed the Atlantic four times with her husband and tells her brother: "We none of us expect to be in smooth water all our days." The reins are with one, the other sits alongside and calmly corrects, and nobody is a passenger.

The first ending of the novel rested on a push from outside: the Admiral makes Wentworth speak up, and Wentworth does so "speaking only for another, and speaking by necessity". Austen thought the scene "tame and flat" and rewrote it. In the new one Wentworth writes the letter himself: **"I must speak to you by such means as are within my reach."** This is how the tail rewrites a couple too: from someone else's push to a step of one's own.

What changes the script: offering the sacrifice rather than making it; speaking for oneself, without go-betweens; not judging a past decision by the wheel's present position; naming the route out loud — where the two are going, who is driving now, when they change over. Control over every step, bans and threats are no longer a lesson of the tail but a reason to seek help: a psychologist, a crisis line, and in danger a local emergency number.

The strong version of the tail is the one in which the two know how to wait and to give way but no longer mistake it for standing still. At the end Wentworth admits he must "endeavour to subdue my mind to my fortune". The Wheel turns, and the reins belong to both.

unit.title: Reins for two

captions.M: To protect each other at the cost of one's own step
captions.N: To live through turns that move the two around
captions.D: To tell firmness from stubbornness and drive together

unit.meaning: Your task is to decide and travel together: no silent sacrifices for the other, no pulling the reins your own way.
